lesson.title: Percentile: Locating a Value Within the Whole Distribution
lesson.summary: A percentile tells you what percentage of the data in a distribution falls at or below a given value, turning a raw score into a statement about its position relative to everyone else.
lesson.body:
A percentile answers a specific question: out of the whole data set, what share of values are at or below this particular one? Formally, the pth percentile of a data set is a value such that p percent of the observations fall at or below it. This idea depends directly on relative frequency, the proportion of observations that fall into a given category or below a given point, applied cumulatively as you move up through the sorted data.

The median, which you already know as the middle value of an ordered data set, is exactly the 50th percentile: by definition, half the data fall at or below the median and half fall at or above it. Percentiles generalize this same idea to any percentage, not just 50. The 25th percentile marks the point below which a quarter of the data fall, the 90th percentile marks the point below which ninety percent of the data fall, and so on, giving a full map of position throughout the distribution rather than just its center.

Consider ten quiz scores, already sorted from lowest to highest: 62, 65, 68, 70, 72, 75, 78, 80, 85, and 90. To find the percentile rank of the score 80, count how many of the ten values are at or below 80: that is 62, 65, 68, 70, 72, 75, 78, and 80 itself, which is 8 values out of 10. Dividing 8 by 10 gives 0.80, so a score of 80 sits at the 80th percentile of this data set, meaning 80 percent of the scores in the set are at or below it. For comparison, the median of this same data set is the average of the fifth and sixth sorted values, 72 and 75, which is 73.5, the 50th percentile marker.

This cumulative counting is exactly what a cumulative relative frequency represents, expressed as a percentage instead of a proportion. Every time you compute a running total of relative frequencies as you move through sorted data, you are building the percentiles for that data set one value at a time. Notice, too, that percentile is purely about position in the sorted order, not about distance: moving from the 10th percentile to the 20th percentile does not necessarily represent the same change in raw values as moving from the 80th percentile to the 90th percentile, especially in a skewed distribution.

Percentiles show up constantly outside the classroom, from standardized test score reports to pediatric growth charts, precisely because they translate an otherwise meaningless raw number into an immediately understandable statement about relative position. Knowing a baby's weight is at the 40th percentile, or that a test score is at the 95th percentile, tells you something a raw number alone cannot: where that observation falls compared to everyone else in the group. A percentile also does not require assuming the distribution looks like a bell curve, which makes it a genuinely resistant, distribution free way to describe position, unlike some of the tools introduced next.

This same relative positioning idea, describing one value's distance from the rest of a distribution, reappears in a different but related form with z-scores. Percentiles and z-scores both answer a version of the question of how one value compares to the rest of the group, but they get there in very different ways: a percentile counts how many observations fall at or below a value, while a z-score measures how many standard deviations away from the mean that value sits.
